case_source: (From the Judgment and Order dated 3-4-79 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 438 of 1978).
full_judgment:
Ruhul Islam, J: - This appeal by special leave arises from the judgment of the High Court Division dated April 3, 1979 in Writ Petition No. 438 of 1978 discharging the Rule obtained by the appellant challenging validity of the order of the respondent at removing him from service.

<u>2. The appellant’s case in short, is that he was appointed by the Trading Corporation of Bangladesh on December 18, 1972 and was posted as the Store Officer at the Head Office in Dacca and I put in charge of 6 to 7 god owns situated in different parts of the city. On April 30, 1976 was transferred to the Regional Office at Chittagong as Stores Officer and while he was serving there he received a show-cause notice on April 16, 1977 alleging miss-appropriation of synthetic fabrics of the value of Tk. 8,896/- from the god own at Siddique Bazar, Dacca. The appellant was charge-sheeted for misconduct and corruption under sub-rules (b) and (c) of Rule 3 of the Government Servants (Discipline and Appeals) Rules, 1976. He showed cause to the charges and in reply he explained to the Enquiry Officer about his innocence and denying the allegations altogether, 1 he Enquiry Officer submitted his report finding him guilty of negligence with a recommendation for giving him warning to refrain from such negligence of duties in future. The Enquiry Officer further recommended that if such negligence was detected in future he should be removed from the service of the Corporation under Rule 4 of the Government Servants (Discipline and Appeals) Rules, 1976 as adopted by the Trading Corporation of Bangladesh.</u>

<u>3. The Enquiry Officer examined six witnesses in support of the charges framed and their evidence was taken in the absence of the appellant. After the inquiry report the appellant was provisionally removed from service by the Corporation and he was asked to show cause why the provisioned decision of his removal from service should not be confirmed. The appellant submitted his reply duly but the management confirmed the provisionally decision which was communicated to him under the memorandum dated April 13, 1978 removing the appellant from service of the Corporation with immediate effect. This order was challenged by filing a writ petition contending inter alia that the appellant was not given any personal hearing either by the Enquiry Officer nor by the Chairman of the Corporation at any stage of the departmental proceeding and he was removed from service without considering the recommendation of the Enquiry Officer. It was further contended that the departmental proceedings were taken in his absence and witnesses were examined and their statements recorded also in his absence and thereby violating the principles of natural justice.</u>

<u>4. From. the judgment of the High Court Division it appears that the learned Judges accepted the statement of the appellant that he was not given personal hearing either by the Enquiry Officer or by the Chairman of the Corporation; and that witnesses were examined in his absence, but the learned Judges, however, did not consider it a fit case for granting the relief prayed for on the ground that examination of witnesses in the absence of the appellant and concluding the proceedings without allowing him to cross-examine the witnesses, did not cause any violation of the principles of natural justice. The learned Judges held that for taking disciplinary measures against a delinquent officer in the absence of any statutory rule making examination or cross-examination of witnesses or giving personal hearing to the delinquent officer mandatory compliance of, the principles of natural justice are limited only to giving him an opportunity to show cause why be shall not be punished for the allegations brought against him The learned Judges observed that "If a detailed enquiry according to the procedure followed in a Court of law is contemplated then statutory rules embodying these requirements will be superfluous, principles of natural justice taking their place." According to the learned Judges the appellant was not condemned unheard.</u>

<u>5. Leave was granted to examine whether the High Court Division was correct in taking the view that-</u>

<u>(1) Requirements of compliance of the principles of natural justice are not applicable to the case of departmental proceedings, not held under any statutory rules;</u>

<u>(2) Government Servants (Disciplinary and Appeals) Rules, 1976 having been adopted by the Bangladesh Trading Corporation and charge-sheet having been framed under the said rules, could it be said that the appellant was found guilty in a domestic inquiry which was not held under statutory rules; and</u>

<u>(3) the principles of natural justice in case of the appellant only required the allegations should be brought to his notice and he should be given an opportunity to submit his defense and if the authority not satisfied with his explanation, his case would be disposed of without holding any inquiry and on consideration of his explanation.</u>

<u>6. For maintaining an application under Article 102 of the Constitution challenging legality of the order of dismissal, the aggrieved person must show that the employer is an 'authority' as contemplated under clause (i) or Article 102 or the Constitution. If the employer is an authority', any order passed in violation of the principles of natural justice can be effectively challenged by a writ petition. In this case the employer is the Bangladesh Trading Corporation which is a statutory body. Therefore, Bangladesh Trading Corporation being undoubtedly an authority,' The applicability of the principles or natural justice does not depend upon the fact that' the proceedings are held under statutory rules or not. In such a case, irrespective of the authority's framing any rules, in an enquiry held against an employee on the charges framed against him for dismissal from service, the principles of natural justice must be complied with.</u>

7. Mr. Rafiq-ul Huq, the learned Counsel, appearing for the appellant has rightly submitted that it does not lie in the month of the employer, namely, the Bangladesh Trading Corporation to contend that the writ petition against the order of dismissal was not maintainable, because, the order of dismissal was passed on the recommendation of the domestic inquiry which was not held under any statutory rules. He submitted with reference to the charge-sheets dated April 6', 1977 and April 25, 1977, Annexure 'A' and, 'B' respectively to the writ petition. That the proceedings were drawn up against the appellant on the charge of misconduct and corruption under sub-rules (b) and (c) of Rule 3 of the Government Servants (Discipline and Appeals) Rules, 1976. The learned Counsel further submitted that the Trading Corporation. Which is a statutory Corporation, instead or framing its own Rules containing the provisions of conditions of service of its employee, adopted the Government Servant (Discipline and Appeals) Rules? 1976 for the purpose and the inquiry was held under the said Rules.

<u>8. The charge-sheet dated April 6, 1977 shows that the Chairman of the Bangladesh Trading Corporation himself signed the charge-sheet alleging that it was prima facie proved that the appellant, misappropriated the synthetic fabric from the go down in connivance with five chowkidars and thereby he was guilty of the charge of misconduct and corruption in terms of sub-rule (b) and (c) of Rule 3 of the Government Servants (Discipline and Appeals) Rules, 1976; and the appellant was directed to show cause as to why he shall not be removed from the service of the Corporation and a sum of Tk. 83.096/00 shall not be realized from him or otherwise suitably punished under Rule 4 of the aforesaid Rules. The appellant was asked to submit his written explanation to the Enquiry Officer within 10 days of receipt of the notice. The appellant was given another notice to show cause 'Why he should not be removed from service on the ground of misconduct and corruption in terms of sub-rule (b) and (c) of Rule 3 of Government Servant s (Discipline and Appeals) Rules, 1976, and a sum of Tk. 83,096/00 should not be realised from him or otherwise suitably punished under Rule 4 of the said Rules. The show-cause notice dated November 26, 1977 was signed by the Chairman himself. By this notice appellant was informed that on the basis of the inquiry reports from the Inquiry Officer of the proceeding drawn up against him the management had provisionally decided to remove him from the service of the Corporation. By enclosing a copy of the inquiry reports, the appellant was directed to explain for the second time in writing within one month of receipt of the letter as to why provisional decision of removal from service should not be confirmed. The appellant submitted his explanation. Then came the impugned order dated April 13, 1978 removing him from the service of the Corporation finding him responsible of the theft of III rolls of synthetic fabric from the godown at Siddique Bazar and thereby causing loss of more or less Tk. 83, 096/00 to the Corporation. The aforesaid notice clearly shows that the domestic proceedings were taken against the appellant under the Government Servant (Discipline and Appeals) Rules, 1976 which the Corporation adopted and this has not been disputed by the Corporation. The High Court Division is wrong in observing that the three recent decisions of this Court, including one reported case in 31 DLR (AD) 33 wherein the question of application of the principles of natural justice has been considered while interpreting Article 7 of the Government of Bangladesh (Services Screening) Order 1972 (P.O. 67 of 1972 are not applicable to the facts of this case. In view of the elaborate proceedings taken under the Rules the contention of Bangladesh Trading Corporation ought not to have been accepted by the High Court Division. It was specifically contended before the High Court Division that the impugned order was passed illegally and in clear violation of the Rules, inasmuch as the appellant was not given any personal hearing either by the Enquiry Officer or by the Chairman of the Corporation at any stage of the proceeding. It was further contended that the appellant was removed from service without following the recommendation of the Enquiry Officer. In short, the main grievance of the appellant was that he was removed from service on the basis of departmental proceedings taken in his absence and witnesses examined and their statements recorded also in his absence and thereby violating the principles of natural justice.</u>

<u>9. We do not find any authority for the view taken by the High Court Division that the Bangladesh Trading Corporation was not bound to hold an enquiry and got power to dispose of the case on consideration of the explanations submitted by the delinquent employee. We also do not find any authority to support the proposition that if any enquiry was held there was no requirement of law that witnesses should be examined in the presence of the delinquent employee or that he should be allowed to cross-examine the witnesses. The High Court Division however, made an observation as under:</u>

<u>"For these are requirements of statutes and not requirement of principles of natural justice, as to personal hearing it is also not a requirement of the principles of natural justice."</u>

<u>We also do not find any authority for ma- king the following observations:</u>

<u>"Be that as it may, in a case like the petitioner where there are no statutory rules making examination or cross-examination of witnesses or personal hearing of an accused mandatory, but disciplinary measures against him are governed by the principles of natural justice, requirements of principles of natural justice are limited to giving him an opportunity to show cause why he will not be punished for the allegations as brought against him. If a detailed enquiry according to the procedures followed in a Court of law as contemplated then statutory rules embodying these requirements will be superfluous principles of natural justice taking their place."</u>

<u>With great respect to the opinion of the learned Judges of the High Court Division we do not approve of the view expressed by them in the matter of an application of principles of natural justice in a domestic enquiry held. by an authority constituted under the statutes. We find that the observations are contrary to the views taken by this Division in connection with the applicability of the principles of natural justice in a departmental proceeding. The Enquiry Officer found the appellant guilty of negligence and recommended for administering a warning for future laches but the appointing authority considered that removed of the petitioner was warranted in the facts and circumstances of the case. While the appointing authority is not bound to accept the recommendation of the enquiry Officer, but in inflicting a higher punishment the appointing authority is expected to assign some reasons for coming to such a decision. There are good authorities for the proposition hat in such case when no reason has been given by the appointing authority, the impugned, order is not immune from attack being vocative of the principles of natural justice, Hence on this ground also the impugned order of dismissal is liable to be declared illegal.</u>

<u>With these observations the appeal is allowed with costs and the judgment of the High Court Division is set aside. The impugned order dated April 13, 1978 dismissing the appellant from service is declared to have been passed without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect.</u>

End.
